note: draft.roles backfilled 2026-08-17 (claude — DRAFT, unreviewed). The three imported essays were the only ones in the set with roles:null, so the paragraph-role work the annotations README ranks second could never use the oldest third of the corpus. Roles need no retrieval — they are a reading of the text — so they are the one thing about 01-03 a cloud run can honestly add. Verdicts are deliberately left null: judging whether the literature supports these claims needs a search, this machine cannot reach the providers (see the note in eval/annotations/README.md), and inventing a verdict from memory is exactly the guessing the null convention exists to prevent. P2 is the arguable one: it asserts a run of unevidenced governing claims and then closes on them, so it does the work of both `claim` and `conclusion` in five sentences. Labelled `claim` because the assertions are what the paragraph is for and the closing sentence restates rather than concludes.

claims.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., yet the majority of public high schools in the United States still begin before that.
claims.note: AAP 2014 recommendation / majority still start before 8:30

claims.text: Teenagers require between eight and ten hours of sleep per night, and roughly 70 percent of them get less than seven.
claims.note: Teens need 8–10 hours, ~70% get under seven

claims.text: The consequence is not subtle: pushing start times later has been shown to increase how long students sleep, and districts that made the change saw fewer car crashes among teen drivers.
claims.note: Later start times → more sleep, fewer crashes

claims.text: Studies show that this sleep debt is the primary driver of the adolescent mental health crisis, and experts agree that smartphones have made it worse.
claims.note: Sleep debt is the primary driver of the mental health crisis

claims.text: If schools do not act, depression rates among teenagers will double within the next decade.
claims.note: Depression rates will double within the next decade
